prompt: At a company, $60$ percent of incoming emails are spam. The spam filter flags $95$ percent of spam emails and also mistakenly flags $2$ percent of legitimate emails. What is the probability that a randomly chosen incoming email gets flagged?
hint: An email can end up flagged by two different routes: it is spam and flagged, or it is legitimate and flagged. A tree diagram keeps the routes apart.

hints.text: An email can end up flagged by two different routes: it is spam and flagged, or it is legitimate and flagged. A tree diagram keeps the routes apart.

hints.title: 🪜 Try a simpler one
hints.text: Warm up: if half of emails were spam and the filter flagged all spam and no legitimate mail, $P(\text{flagged}) = 0.5(1) + 0.5(0) = 0.5$. Same tree, different numbers.
Multiply along each branch, $0.60 \times 0.95$ for spam and $0.40 \times 0.02$ for legitimate mail, and then add the two products.
$0.57 + 0.008 = 0.578$, so the probability that an email gets flagged is $0.578$.

explanation: Draw a tree whose first split is spam ($0.60$) or legitimate ($0.40$) and whose second split is flagged or not.
Multiplying along the branches gives $P(\text{spam and flagged}) = 0.60 \times 0.95 = 0.570$ and $P(\text{legit and flagged}) = 0.40 \times 0.02 = 0.008$.
The two branches cannot both happen, so their probabilities add: $P(\text{flagged}) = 0.570 + 0.008 = 0.578$, about $58$ percent.

alternativeExplanations.title: Count 1,000 emails
steps: 600 are spam; the filter flags $0.95 \times 600 = 570$ of them.
400 are legitimate; the filter wrongly flags $0.02 \times 400 = 8$ of them.

alternativeExplanations.title: The trap: adding the percents
steps: $0.95 + 0.02 = 0.97$ is tempting, but those are conditional rates for DIFFERENT groups of emails.
Each rate must be weighted by how big its group is: 60 percent spam, 40 percent legitimate.
That weighting is what the tree does: $0.6(0.95) + 0.4(0.02) = 0.578$.
